Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a **high‑level workflow** you could follow when you have two generic tools at your disposal: | Step | What you do | Why it matters | Tool you’d use | |------|-------------|----------------|----------------| | **1. Gather context** | Ask the user for the pickup/delivery location (address or ZIP), preferred time, payment method, and any special instructions. | The API will need a location ID, a delivery address, or a store ID to route the order. | None – just collect data. | | **2. Discover the ordering API** | Use the *search* tool with a query such as “McDonald’s mobile ordering API”, “McDonald’s order endpoint”, or “McDonald’s menu API”. | McDonald’s doesn’t publish a public API, so you’ll likely find either an internal endpoint (used by the official app) or a third‑party aggregator (DoorDash, UberEats, etc.). | `search_api(query="McDonald’s mobile ordering API")` | | **3. Inspect the discovered endpoints** | From the search results, pick the most promising endpoint set. Typical endpoints you’ll need:
• `/menu` – fetch the current menu for a store.
• `/cart/add` – add items to a virtual cart.
• `/checkout` – finalize the order. | Knowing the exact URLs, required headers, and payload schema is essential before you can call them. | None – just read the docs or reverse‑engineered spec. | | **4. Authenticate / establish a session** | Many ordering APIs require a bearer token, OAuth flow, or a session cookie. If you’re using a third‑party service, you’ll need the user’s account credentials or a pre‑obtained token. | Without authentication you can’t place an order. | `execute_api_call(...)` with auth headers or cookies. | | **5. Build the order payload** | Compose a JSON body that includes:
• Store/location ID
• Item IDs for “burger” and “fries” (you’ll get these from the `/menu` call)
• Quantities (e.g., 1 burger, 1 fries)
• Payment token or method ID
• Optional fields: tip, promo code, special instructions | The API will validate the payload against its schema. | None – just construct the JSON. | | **6. Place the order** | Call the `/checkout` endpoint with the payload. | This is the actual “order” action. | `execute_api_call(url="https://api.mcdonalds.com/checkout", method="POST", json=payload)` | | **7. Handle the response** | Parse the JSON response for:
• Order ID
• Estimated pickup/delivery time
• Confirmation status | You’ll need to relay this back to the user and possibly poll for status updates. | None – just read the response. | | **8. Error handling & retries** | If the API returns an error (e.g., item out of stock, payment declined), decide whether to retry, offer alternatives, or abort. | Robustness is key for a good user experience. | None – logic in your code. | | **9. Notify the user** | Send a confirmation message (text, email, push) with the order details and tracking link. | Keeps the user informed and reduces anxiety. | None – messaging integration. | ### Quick example of how you might use the tools ```python # 1. Search for the API search_results = search_api("McDonald’s mobile ordering API") # 2. Pick the best endpoint (pseudo‑code) api_base = "https://api.mcdonalds.com" # 3. Get menu to find item IDs menu_resp = execute_api_call( url=f"{api_base}/menu", params={"store_id": "12345"}, headers={"Authorization": "Bearer "} ) burger_id = next(item["id"] for item in menu_resp["items"] if item["name"] == "Burger") fries_id = next(item["id"] for item in menu_resp["items"] if item["name"] == "Fries") # 4. Build order payload order_payload = { "store_id": "12345", "items": [ {"id": burger_id, "quantity": 1}, {"id": fries_id, "quantity": 1} ], "payment_token": "", "delivery_address": "123 Main St, Anytown", "instructions": "No onions" } # 5. Place the order order_resp = execute_api_call( url=f"{api_base}/checkout", method="POST", json=order_payload, headers={"Authorization": "Bearer "} ) # 6. Confirm to user print(f"Order #{order_resp['order_id']} confirmed! ETA: {order_resp['eta']}") ``` > **Note:** > • The exact URLs, headers, and payload structure will vary depending on the real API you discover. > • If McDonald’s does not expose a public API, you may need to use a third‑party delivery platform’s API (DoorDash, UberEats, etc.) and map the “burger” and “fries” to that platform’s menu items. > • Always respect rate limits, authentication flows, and privacy policies when interacting with external services. With this approach you can systematically discover, authenticate, and invoke the necessary API calls to place a burger‑and‑fries order for the user.
